items.content:
Under Google Play’s global developer policies, all active developer accounts must declare whether they are a trader or non-trader under European Economic Area (EEA) and United Kingdom (UK) laws in Play Console. This declaration must be completed by February 1, 2027, regardless of where apps are targeted or distributed. The declaration must reflect whether you engage in commercial activities that classify you as a trader. You are solely legally responsible for ensuring that your declaration remains accurate, truthful, and current at all times.

: If you don’t distribute apps in the European Economic Area or the United Kingdom, you can declare as a non-trader.

Under applicable laws, a trader is any natural or legal person acting for purposes relating to their trade, business, craft or profession. If you are acting outside of these purposes (such as a personal hobby or other non-commercial activity), you are unlikely to be a trader.

How to determine if you're a trader

To help you determine if your activities classify you as a trader, you may consider the following non-exhaustive list of criteria from the European Commission guidance (Section 2.2, "The concept of trader"):

  • : you receive or intend to receive remuneration for your apps (for example, paid apps, in-app purchases, ad-sponsored apps) on a regular or commercial basis.
  • : you have a high or consistent number, amount, or frequency of transactions.
  • : you manage your app development and publishing as a business.
  • : you have a legal status (such as a D-U-N-S number) that enables you to engage in commercial activities

In countries and regions where displaying trader status is required (for example, the EEA and the UK), your declaration will be visible to consumers. If you declare yourself as a "non-trader," we will inform consumers in these regions that consumer rights stemming from consumer protection laws do not apply to contracts between you and them. Note that under the EU Unfair Commercial Practices Directive (UCPD) and the UK Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act (DMCCA), it is strictly prohibited to falsely claim or create the impression that you are not acting as a trader, and doing so may result in global removal.

: This page is for informational guidance only and does not constitute legal advice. Google cannot evaluate your business activities or provide legal determinations of your trader status. If you are unsure whether you qualify as a trader, we recommend consulting with a legal professional.

How to declare your trader or non-trader status

Declare trader status for your account

First, set your account-level trader status settings:

  1. Sign in to Google Play Console.
  2. Go to > > .
  3. Follow the on-screen prompts to declare your trader status for your overall account.

Confirm trader status for each app

If you are a trader, confirm the trader status for each app in your portfolio:

  1. Sign in to Google Play Console and select your app.
  2. In the left navigation, go to > > .
  3. Confirm the trader status for that app

Additional steps you need to take if you’re a trader

If you declare as a trader, you will be asked to self-certify that you commit to only offer products or services that comply with applicable laws. You will also be asked to provide the link to the terms of service for each of your apps.

If you use a personal developer account, you must provide a contact phone number to be displayed on Google Play. Be aware that your address will also be publicly displayed.

To keep your apps available on Google Play, make sure your trader status declaration matches your account’s and apps’ activity. If you’ve declared as a non-trader but we detect activity that indicates you may qualify as a trader, we may ask you to confirm or update your status. If you don’t respond within the specified timeframe, your apps may be removed from Google Play.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why do I need to submit a trader status declaration?

To support Google Play’s transition to an online marketplace model in the EEA and the UK effective March 1, 2027, Google Play policies require all developers worldwide to declare their trader status. This ensures that the correct consumer protection information is provided to users in those regions.

Can I change my trader status after declaring?

Yes. If your business model or app distribution details change (for example, you begin or cease engaging in commercial activities), you can update your declaration at any time in Play Console.

What happens if I don’t complete the declaration?

Failure to declare your trader status by the February 1, 2027 deadline may trigger enforcement including app update blocks and removal from the Play Store globally.

Misrepresenting your trader status (for example, declaring non-trader status to bypass verification or self-certification) violates the representations and warranties in Section 11.4 of the DDA and may result in account suspension or termination globally under Section 10.3 (a) of the DDA.

What is the deadline to declare whether I am a trader?

All new developer accounts are required to submit the declaration immediately upon account creation. Existing developer accounts must submit the declaration by February 1, 2027.

I already went through the developer verification D-U-N-S process, why am I doing it again?

The trader status declaration is separate to the existing developer identity verification process. The identity verification is a blanket requirement used to collect and verify information about every developer regardless of their trader status. You are not re-doing the D-U-N-S verification; instead, if you are a trader, the D-U-N-S number you already provided will be displayed to users on your app's detail page.

What happens if I declare as a trader? What else gets shown to users in the Play store?

When you declare as a trader, you will be asked to self-certify that you commit to offering products or services that comply with local laws.

Starting March 1, 2027, users everywhere will see:

  • : Your contact details will be shown. Notably, if you have an individual account and are a trader, a phone number and address will now be displayed.
  • : Your D-U-N-S number will be displayed in the "App support" section.
  • : A link to your app’s Terms of Service, if you provided one.

Starting March 1, 2027, users in the EEA and UK will also see:

  • : Your developer/trader name will replace Google in the "Offered by" field of the "About this app" section.
  • : Your commitment to offer products or services compliant with local laws will be displayed.

items.title: Novita, StreamLake, etc. are ByteDance Ark wrappers
items.author: leafingensemble
items.content:
Sit back, but you probably won't be able to relax - this one's a doozy. First, , who looks like a standard US ZDR inference provider at first:

Zero Data Retention is the default for all endpoints, including serverless API calls.

But the more you look, the weirder it gets. Why did OpenRouter drop their ZDR status sometime before ? Why is their family tree so complicated?

  • PPLabs Technology Limited
    • PPLabs HK
      • Shanghai DAO
        • PPIO Shanghai PPIO 派欧云

And who are their subprocessors? Many ( 45.8%) think they would have none, since most OpenRouter providers host models themselves. And PPLabs's draft IPO assures:

A defining feature of our model API services is that we do not simply provide a pass-through gateway to underlying models.

You understand and agree that, [for] the large-model API product, third-party technical-support providers provide the large-model API. PPIO makes no warranty of any kind regarding the large-model API, whether express or implied, including but not limited to its authenticity, suitability, non-infringement and security. Furthermore, regarding the third-party technical-support providers' large-model API, PPIO will not participate in the development and operation of the large-model API; PPIO only provides a neutral platform and related technical services.

I also contacted their support and privacy contacts, and all they told me as of writing is that models labeled as "Partner" may go to Qwen and InclusionAI. You can't get a straight answer.

What about ? It's Kuaishou's model platform, and it looks like a host too. But some of its error messages aren't StreamLake's. They're word for word Novita's gateway errors: invalid request error trace_id: …. And on GLM 5.3 Flash, it sometimes returns a tool-call id format ( + 16 hex digits) that only Novita produces, out of 41 hosts. Why would StreamLake's requests come back from Novita?

It keeps going. passes through StreamLake's own request ids ( + 6 characters + 19 digits) on V4.1 Flash, V4 Pro and GLM 5. And then there's , a Singapore subsidiary of Ant Group that listed DeepSeek V4.1 Flash on November 18 at "60% off", with ZDR (until OpenRouter removed it on November 22), and went from 1B tokens a day to 35.8B on November 21. Where is all this actually going?

The MiniMax investigation

You might've already seen OpenRouter's notice that requests sent to MiniMax models "may have been read". A security researcher put unique URLs in prompts, and a third party opened them 40 to 130 hours later. This happened even with non-MiniMax providers:

AtlasCloud, Novita and StreamLake have told us they forwarded OpenRouter requests for MiniMax models to MiniMax.

So the forwarding is admitted. MiniMax's own notice names the same three and says its security system, on by default, opened URLs from forwarded requests, ZDR ones included. Novita's notice calls it a "routing configuration issue" on a path "intended for specific customers", and promises better "Partner API labeling", the same "Partner" label its support told me means a request goes to Qwen or inclusionAI. Since then, 16 of Novita's endpoints have come off OpenRouter: every Qwen and inclusionAI model, plus StepFun, Tencent and all but one Kimi.

But MiniMax is a very small model series. What about DeepSeek?

Ark is ByteDance's model API: Volcano Engine Ark in mainland China, BytePlus ModelArk everywhere else. It sells DeepSeek, GLM and Kimi, and it leaves fingerprints:

  • Who downloads your images. StreamLake's V4.1 Flash images are downloaded from Beijing Volcano Engine (AS137718), ByteDance's cloud. Ant Digital's pass through Ant's own gateway on Alibaba Cloud, then get downloaded by , BytePlus in Singapore. Novita's own API used to do the same (, Volcano Engine, on November 12), until Novita started downloading images itself first, from AWS.
  • Every Ant Digital response's upstream ID is a ByteDance one: + a millisecond timestamp + hex.
  • Novita's and StreamLake's V4.1 Flash return Ark's format ( + 24 lowercase letters and digits).
  • Ask StreamLake's V4 Pro 0813 who Tank Man was, or Novita's GLM 5.1 about June 4, 1989, and you can get ByteDance's canned refusal: ("Hello, I can't provide related content.")
  • Ant Digital launched at $0.12/$0.48 per million tokens, exactly BytePlus's off-peak "Economy" rate for that model. By November 25 it was down to $0.09/$0.36, below BytePlus's own list price.

Other tests, which I won't detail here, put Novita's V4 Pro 0813 and V4.1 Flash 1017 on BytePlus in Singapore and its V4.1 Flash on Volcano Engine in Beijing, as of November 21. That's the chart at the top: Novita alone sent 120-160B tokens a day on these models until it lost its ZDR label on November 20, then 33B on November 21. Routes move, though; one of those changed within an afternoon, and Novita's V4.1 Flash 1017 had stopped showing Ark's fingerprints by November 24. As for the weird errors, part of StreamLake's traffic goes through Novita on its way to ByteDance. So a V4.1 Flash request to SiliconFlow can go SiliconFlow → StreamLake → Novita → ByteDance.

Bonus: Novita's "DeepSeek V4 Pro" isn't the original V4 Pro. On Novita's own API, it sometimes answers with DeepSeek's for the 0813 checkpoint (). ByteDance sells 0813 as "DeepSeek-V4-Pro正式版" (V4 Pro GA) and marks the original as about to be retired.

Why bother? Price. BytePlus advertises savings plans of 30-50% off for high volume, and the clouds come to you: Morph's Tejas Bhakta posted a Tencent Cloud email offering "up to 50-60% off" to route requests to them.

Attested proof of the image downloads, request IDs, tool-call IDs and refusals is available here (run 44960395726 on 6dbc036). It asks every OpenRouter host of DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, so you can compare against everyone else too.

While a grant from OpenRouter helped with the research here and I work for an employer who would prefer to go unnamed, this post does not represent or reflect anyone else's opinion - it is simply research I am publishing.

Thanksgiving update: MOAT

Command Code advertises MOAT as a way "to access the highest quality models at wholesale prices", with "ZERO router fee" and "no processing fee". They charge you a processing fee anyway:

1 credit = $1 of usage. Credits never expire.

Where do your requests go? Command Code's privacy policy names Anthropic, OpenAI, Vercel, Cloudflare and OpenRouter as its AI subprocessors. But the endpoint its CLI uses reports which provider answered, and for 14 of its 122 models, the answer is sometimes or always Novita.

Turning on zero data retention () sends more of your traffic there, not less. DeepSeek V4.1 Flash is around 8% Novita with ZDR off but around 91% Novita with it on. Kimi K3, Kimi K3.1 Pro, Ling 3.1, GLM-5.3 FlashX and Hy3 go to Novita either way. (And when Command Code routes to Vercel, Vercel sometimes routes to Command Code's Novita BYOK. Command Code says even when Vercel calls Novita .) Attested proof is available here (run 46047915789 on 9021bfe).

items.title: NormalScript: A perfectly normal scripting language
items.author: hn-aarvin
items.content:
Runtime.make({ globals, limits }) returns a runtime. globals is called for each run, and again on resume, with the run's id and metadata. Globals shadow built-ins of the same name.
A sync host function returns its value to the script directly. An async one gives the script a promise at once. Host calls may run concurrently. Host.fail gives the script a catchable error with your own kind.
{ ok: true, value } or { ok: false, error: { kind, message, suggestions? } }, plus console logs, warnings, and the run's metadata. The value crosses as JSON.stringify would serialize it.
Two options, neither set by default. timeoutMs is active time, summed across resumes and checked between VM steps; a single regular-expression match runs on the host engine and is not interrupted. maxOutputBytes is the UTF-8 bytes kept from the result and logs, with an equal budget for warnings; the rest is cut. There is no separate memory or step-count limit.
Strings: 2^24 characters. Arrays: 10,000,000 elements. Pending promises: 10,000. Nesting across the host boundary: 32 levels. Exceeding a cap throws a RangeError in the script.
Aborting the signal passed to execute() or program.run() aborts every host call's call.signal and rejects the run with an AbortError. A host call that ignores its signal is not waited for.
suspend() returns the run's state; toBytes() and fromBytes() turn it into bytes and back. A snapshot resumes on the build that wrote it. Another build, or malformed bytes, rejects with a SnapshotError. suspend({ maxBytes }) caps the size. Store snapshots as you would store code.
Host calls during suspend
An async call marked idempotent runs again on resume with the same call.key. Otherwise suspend() rejects with a SuspendError while the call is in progress, and the run goes on.
Host.durableFn work keeps running across a suspend. start() returns JSON kept in the snapshot, wait() gets the result, again after a resume, and cancel() runs if the run ends without it.
Runs are deterministic except for Math.random(), Date.now(), new Date() with no arguments, crypto.randomUUID(), and crypto.getRandomValues(). There is no option to seed them. A host may shadow them with globals; the replacement is the whole object.
Optional. The /effect entry point exports the same names with an Effect API. Host functions may return Effects, and interrupting a run interrupts its host calls. The Promise API has no dependency on Effect.

items.title: Deploying a payphone on a tiny Pacific Island for fun and zero profit
items.author: qzervaas
items.content:
For the past few years Australia’s Telstra has run a campaign of “Free calls to Santa” from the universal service obligation funded payphones across the country – It’s a really fun idea and we wanted to replicate it on our network on Norfolk Island where we run the mobile network, but the’s no payphones.*

* There is now a payphone – You probably already guessed this.

Getting a Payphone to a small island in the South Pacific

Step 1 was getting a payphone.

Those who have seen my office / shed / studio / the HackHouse, know that I may have one or two payphones… But this needed a payphone that could stand the elements and be modern ish.

The answer, is of course, to use the sexiest payphone of all time; the . Featuring VFD display, durable keypad, card service, coin service, no fancy metering line required.

Unfortunately Nortel’s bankruptcy in 2008 meant I couldn’t phone up an account manager, but with the hookup of some guy with a U-Haul van full of Millennium’s in the US and a bit of a road trip, Cody from our team managed to pickup some really clean GTE branded payphones for the job.

Then Cody flew to Sydney where we drove to the house of someone who was heading to Norfolk the next day to explain they’d need to leave all their baggage at home as all of their baggage allowance was to be taken up with the weight of a payphone – Thanks Paul.

Eventually with the Payphone on Norfolk, we needed to get it programmed; for that there’s Howard Harte’s great , which, with the aid of a USB modem is able to program the phones.

I hit a bit of a stumbling block with as the software assumed you were part of the North American Numbering Plan (NANP) – as one of the literally of people who live outside of America, having to put a in front of the number wasn’t going to fly.

After some trial and error I sussed out what bits on the config files that get pushed to the phone controls this and submitted a PR to which is now merged.

We’re also able to set the messaging that appears on the screen, which I’m very happy with the branding on.

We set it for free-on-net calls, so anyone can call any Norfone number without charge and the Payphone tag number.

Once this would’ve been the hard part, I did some work a long time ago with IBM Watson and built some stuff to annoy voters via phone with automated phone calls and capture their human responses and sort them and play the appropriate response. But tech has come a long way since 2019, and this was the easy part of the project.

We setup the payphone to make HOHOHO (464646) a destination that did not require coins when we did the rating table setup when programming the phone.

The ATA the payphone is connected to just comes through to our IMS like any other fixed line subscriber; the TAS is setup to zero-rate the destination and then it’s dialplan forwards it to “Santa Bridge” listening for SIP on port 5090.

I’ve got 4 pre-recorded “Norfolk Specific” greetings to buy us time to get everything setup in the background, once these greetings play (each ends asking the caller their name) then we feed into the OpenAI API.

One of the members from our team attempted to ask Santa to write a Python script to iterate over a , while another team member asked Santa for firearms. In both cases it did a good job of redirecting.

The phone came GTE branded, so we needed to redo the card with the branding on it that goes around the screen. Two screws and some wiggling later we pulled out the card, and then I badgered my partner into using their day off to design a new one, with a retro style I really like.

The install was beautifully completed by long-time-reader-of-the-blog Minas from Shield Electrical and Air.

He knocked up a housing to it from the rain and elements and installed it outside the office entrance.

Getting it on Payphone Tag

Future payphone adventures

So with this now in place, we’ve still got to give it some tinsel and Christmas cheer, and I’ll get some more pics of it in place.

We’re waiting for someone to claim it on Payphone tag, and we’ve shipped 3 of these to another even more remote Island I’ll hopefully be able to share more info on later.

If you’re ever on Norfolk, give it a call.

I read Koukyosyumei's article "著名なRust製OSSをLean 4で形式検証してみたら、めちゃめちゃバグが見つかった話" (in Japanese; the title means "I formally verified well-known Rust OSS with Lean 4 and found a lot of bugs"). The author ported well-known Rust projects into a form they could prove in Lean 4, and where a proof failed, they found a bug in the original code.

Many people have used Clojure's persistent data structures since around 1.0, so I expected no bugs to remain. Still, I wanted to see whether Lean would find something there too.

hirosassa/lean-verify describes a procedure for modeling a small function in Lean 4 and checking it for all inputs, so I applied it to the part of Clojure's core written in Java.

I modeled integer and bit arithmetic in Lean and searched for counterexamples. I checked the collections with differential testing against the collections, and for Java interop I compared the same call with and without a type hint.

I found 17 bugs that I could not find in Clojure's JIRA or on ask.clojure.org. They include on , the hash collision node of the HAMT, and calls to functional interfaces without a type hint.

items.title: I've been drinking wine in my kitchen
items.author: nill0
items.content:
See I don’t even alcohol much. Like, I’ll have a half-glass of wine at a fancy dinner if everyone else is having some, or one beer at a reception, but that’s it. These days, though, can you blame me?

Yesterday, as you all probably saw, hot on the heels of its proof of the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis, Anthropic released a proof of Valiant’s VP≠VNP conjecture—a central algebraic analogue of the P≠NP conjecture, and considered a “warmup” to proving P≠NP since the late 1970s. Then, later the same day, OpenAI released a proof of the VP≠VNP conjecture as well.

You can read all about the VP vs. VNP problem in Section 6.5 of my P vs. NP survey. But briefly, for those tuning in from home, Valiant’s conjecture says that the permanent of an n×n matrix has no algebraic circuits (that is, circuits built out of addition and multiplication gates and constants) of size polynomial in n, unlike the determinant, which does. Anthropic’s result says that a circuit of size exp(Ω(log n)) is needed, whereas OpenAI gets exp(Ω(log n)): so, more than polynomial albeit less than exponential. As is often the case, the best known upper bound here is ~2. The lower bounds are said to work over all fields of characteristic other than 2. (What’s special about 2? Over a field of characteristic 2, addition and subtraction are the same, so the permanent just the determinant, and is easy to compute!)

From what little I understand so far, the proof techniques in the Anthropic and OpenAI papers look similar. They both do some sort of highly nontrivial “compression” or “shortening,” followed in the end by a diagonalization—the oldest trick in the book! Diagonalization is what should let these arguments evade the infamous natural proofs barrier. There’s probably also a story to tell about how the arguments evade an algebraic-circuit version of the relativization barrier, but I don’t know how to tell it yet.

One immediate implication of these results is that, if you want to map an n×n matrix A to an m×m matrix B whose entries are affine functions of the entries of A, and have the permanent of A be equal to the determinant of B, then m must be exp(Ω(log n)). This was the question directly targeted by Ketan Mulmuley’s Geometric Complexity Theory program—which, however, these papers don’t use, taking a more direct route to the desired lower bound.

As is de rigueur these days, the proofs come with Lean, formally certifying their correctness to a level considerably what we’d normally demand for a math paper published in a journal. If recent experience is any guide, this will not prevent boatloads of morons from denying that AI could have solved these problems, and latching onto anything whatsoever (e.g., unused Lean code or Lean that deviates slightly from the natural-language version) to declare the proofs to be fallacious … and such claims will then go viral, lapped up by an eager audience on Bluesky and other places hungry for AI denial. If there’s any real technical issue with the proofs, I’ll be happy to hear about it from experts, but my patience for arguing with the flat-earthers is at an end.

Daniel Harlow asked me whether the proof of VP≠VNP raises my confidence in P≠NP itself, which I’d lowered from 97% to 95% in light of OpenAI’s and Anthropic’s recent refutation of the Exponential Time Hypothesis. I said sure, I’m now back up to 96%.

The possibility that this will be followed up soon by a proof of P≠NP itself has not escaped my notice, or anyone else’s, not at the AI companies. Will the big one come tomorrow? Next week? Next month? In a year? Who the hell knows? Hence the wine drinking, which I wouldn’t call sad, but just … .

If that wasn’t enough for you—if you still want —yesterday Sanjeev Khanna, Aaron Putterman, and Junkai Song posted an ECCC preprint with a deterministic linear-time algorithm for finding minimum spanning trees in graphs. (The best previously-known algorithm was ridiculously to linear time—n α(n) where α is the inverse of the Ackermann function—but not quite. A linear-time algorithm was known.) This was a huge open problem for decades, and one that my wife Dana spent roughly two years working on.

Khanna et al. write, “the main ideas in [our] paper were entirely generated by AI—specifically 6.2 Astra, on a mixture of Ultra and Max effort—with minimal human intellectual intervention. The authors then worked to first carefully verify, and then to simplify and clarify the treatment.”

Anyway, yeah, tonight I’ll again raise my glass, I’ll pray that at the bottom of this terrifying rollercoaster lies a world that my children and I will be glad to inhabit, and I’ll mutter to myself the eternal words:

God would like us to be joyfulEven though our hearts lie panting on the floor;

How much more can we be joyful,

When there’s really something

To life, to life, l’chaim!L’chaim, l’chaim, to life!

It gives you something to think about,

Something to drink about,

Another Update (Nov. 27): At my suggestion, my friend Václav Rozhoň of the polylog YouTube channel interviewed my other friend Amir Shpilka about the VP versus VNP breakthrough! And the result is awesome! I enjoyed it and learned a few new things! You can watch it here.

items.title: Launch HN: Versine (YC F26) – MCP to send and receive money
items.author: harshithl1777
items.content:
Hey HN, we’re Harshith, Param, and Vishnu and we're building Versine (https://versine.com). Versine lets you send and request money just by talking or texting with your AI (think Venmo with an MCP). We’re software engineers who have worked on distributed systems at Stripe, Databricks, and Amazon.

Versine is an MCP that sits in front of a wallet with a balance. With it, your agent can do things like:

- Send money to someone with your approval (via passkey in our app)

- Send and request money to/from up to 100 people at once

- Send money to people without a Versine account (they cash out to their bank in 2 mins)

- Pay people without your explicit approval to trusted contacts (you can set this)

We started working on this because assistants are frustratingly hands-off when it comes to finance and money movement. You can have your assistant go through a receipt and map out all the amounts owed taking care of splitting the subtotal, taxes, tips, but at the end of it the assistant hands back work to you when you have to go out and make the Venmo transfer.

Our current solution is oriented towards power users: those who want to automate everything through their agent use us to split dinners, group trips, or settle poker ledgers. We see ourselves unlocking more value for the general consumer as

1. More people turn into power users of agents, and 2. We expand to a more complete banking solution: deposits, transfers, wires, everything you can (and more) do with your bank offered as an MCP.

Behind the scenes, each user has a self-custodial stablecoin wallet storing USDC on Base. With self-custodial wallets, users own their keys, meaning money can’t be sent without their approval.

Interestingly, we were almost forced into this solution because we had around 4 weeks to build this product (after a pivot), and traditional fiat with a partner bank would have caused far too many regulatory and compliance slowdowns.

Because of that, the only fast option that remained was using stablecoin wallets. It also ensures we aren't a Money Services Business (MSB) since we don’t hold control or access to the user’s funds.

Each call to the wallet creates what we call one-time or recurring standing permissions. For a one-time payment, your agent makes an MCP call, and you receive a notification in our mobile app. Once you swipe up in the app and approve with a passkey (or your device’s biometric method), we create a one-time permission that instructs your wallet to send $X to your recipient’s address.

Trusted contacts let your agent send money to people that you’ve previously authorized without explicit passkey approval. Generally, these are people that you’d trust to send your money back even if your agent made a mistake.

We’re also able to support sending money to someone off Versine using claim forwarding, where the user authorizes us to forward a specific amount to a future address (which we create once we verify a recipient's OTP).

Param worked on scaling vector search at Databricks and harness evals at Glean. Harshith worked on core Stripe Connect fee-processing infrastructure and built an AWS Fargate autoscaler at Amazon. Vishnu worked on intent-based agent testing infrastructure at Amazon. None of us were experienced in stablecoin or crypto infra before working on Versine but our distributed systems experience has helped us a lot.

We'd love for you guys to try it! It's available on iOS and Android and as an MCP on ChatGPT and Claude. We also support a public MCP and REST API for other agents.

Please let us know how you find it and if it works as you'd hoped!

items.title: Gödel Enigma
items.author: benbreen
items.content:
Gödel's solitary work was the single most important factor in the development of precise theories of formal languages, which, through the coding that he invented, can be handled by a machine. His work led to precise notions of algorithmic computability from which a direct path leads to the first theoretical ideas of a computer in the work of Alan Turing in 1936 and John von Neumann some years later.

The development of logic and foundational study has been known to us only in broad outlines until Jean van Heijenoort's pioneering work. He published in 1967 a collection of original papers under the title From Frege to Gödel: The Development of Mathematical Logic 1879-1931. There was, however, no attempt at organised historical work with the sources. Such detailed work is still in a very early state and crucial sources for the development of logic remain unexplored.

Deep intellectual history cannot be achieved if only published work is considered.Comparison to a parallel and partly overlapping development is illuminating. Quantum mechanics, as well as foundations of mathematics, received a decisive impetus around the year 1900, with Planck's discovery of the quantum of action, and the discovery of Russell's paradox and Hilbert's idea of formalisation. All of these developments led to a well-established theoretical account by the early 1930s, right before the Nazi takeover in Germany: quantum mechanics in the second part of the 1920s in the work of the Göttingers Heisenberg and Born, logic and foundations with the full development of first-order logic by the early 1930s by the Göttingers Hilbert, Bernays, and Gentzen, assisted mainly by Gödel's striking discoveries.

Historical work on the development of quantum mechanics began in the 1960s in a massive effort in which every conceivable source was unearthed and made available in several hundred microfilm reels, the Archive for the History of Quantum Physics.

Sadly, nothing of this kind was ever done with logic and foundations. Our present information society owes a part of its existence to a well-hidden but essential line of development. There are several thousand pages of notes by Gödel waiting to be studied, written in Similarly, extensive notes for lecture courses during the crucial years, written by Paul Bernays, the central driving force in foundational study around 1930, as well as over five thousand contemporaneous letters exist in the Bernays archive. These have been exploited only sporadically. The fate of many other sources, such as the papers of Gerhard Gentzen and Rose Rand, has been similar.

The main aims of our project are twofold:

  1. To obtain a full, objective picture of Kurt Gödel's crucial role as the logician behind the birth of present information society through a careful study of sources next to published work.
  2. To exploit Gödel's hidden discoveries to the full, an endeavour whose results can be partly foreseen, as with his 1942 proof of independence of the axiom of choice, but in some cases still shrouded in mystery, as with his suggested proof of the independence of the continuum hypothesis "through the Brouwerian method."It should be clear that so far completely unknown scientific developments will surface – one early finding is some thirty years before Fitch's published works .

Understanding Gödel's unpublished papers requires a combination of mastery of the logical details and the application of professional standards of historical-foundational research to the source material, which, in addition, is only accessible to a reader trained in stenographic writing. So far, much of this work remains to be done. There are two exceptions: the transcription of Gödel's so-called "Zilsel lecture" in Vienna in January 1938 and his Göttingen lecture on the consistency of the continuum hypothesis of December 1939, both published in the third volume of Gödel's Both of these texts were lecture notes, relatively finished in comparison to the private notes. More recently, much effort has been dedicated to producing transcriptions of Gödel's philosophical notebooks that he called "Max Phil," or in order to better understand Gödel the philosopher. Our project will provide ample material for future generations of philosophers and logicians to complement the picture given by the as well as other works of Gödel's published so far.

The project consists of theoretically oriented basic research. It uses special methods for the study of mostly unpublished primary sources, the contemporary methods of logic and foundational study to aid in their interpretation, up-to-date formal methods for the development of research themes suggested by the sources, and scholarly methodological standards of historical-foundational research.

The main sources comprise a number of series of notebooks, all written in shorthand and logical symbolism, left virtually untouched except for the series:

  1. is a collection of four notebooks continuously numbered from page 1 to 368, with systematically presented results on logic and foundations that Gödel considered to be in a final form. These were written in a relatively short time span between 1942 and 1943.
  2. is an incredibly rich and complicated series of sixteen notebooks on various logical and mathematical topics, altogether some twelve hundred shorthand pages. Most of the notes have been written between the mid-1930s and mid-1940s.
  3. is a well-organized collection of six notebooks, continuously numbered from page 1 to 440, often referred to simply as . It records Gödel's own work, often in the form of concise surveys, as well as the work by others that Gödel had read.
  4. is a series of 15 notebooks (one lost) of philosophical and foundational observations, written between 1934-1955. Lately, the notebooks and transcriptions exist of most of the notebooks, although they have not been published yet.
  5. Earlier and isolated notebooks. There are many isolated notebooks and diaries, such as the "Amerika 1933/34" and "Amerika 1935" notebooks, as well as a series of earlier , preceding the books, the first entries of which are from the early 1940s. Many of these isolated notebooks call for a separate study.

Gödel's notebooks have some overlap in themes, ideas and results that are presented in or often appearing in less finished form in the Arbeitshefte, to give an example. Gödel was meticulous about keeping his notebooks, and they contain detailed lists of contents from which we can infer that he did reread them. There is a separate list of "Progress" entries, in which he summed both his achievements and objectives in numbered points in the

As of early Spring 2019, our current projects include the following:

  1. Jan von Plato has been occupied by transcribing and translating Gödel's notebooks on incompleteness, the as well as the later The latter two notebooks are a summary of finished work that remained unpublished, a legacy to be. They turned out to be very readable, modulo the archaic Gabelsberger shorthand, with almost no cancellations or hesitation, and a good coverage that makes them largely self-contained for a trained reader. What were Gödel's central aims in logic and foundations at that time, and why did it all remain unpublished?
  2. Annika Kanckos and Tim Lethen have made remarkable discoveries about Gödel's's ontological argument and are preparing a definitive account of this topic. Tim has been digging into the theological notebooks that reveal surprising new aspects of Kurt Gödel. He has also transcribed a diary-type notebook from 1937-38 that gives a unique view of the last days of Viennese intellectual life.
  3. Maria Hämeen-Anttila has been working on Gödel's early results, views, and remarks on intuitionism and constructivity in mathematics, with materials collected from the and other early notebooks. She should be finished with her work, which constitutes her doctoral dissertation, in late spring.
  4. Jan and Maria have edited for publication Gödel's "Princeton Lectures on Intuitionism": These make up to more than a hundred pages. Maria's extensive introduction to the lecture series explains how the notes, written mostly in longhand English, relate to the shorthand of the same time, 1941.

items.title: Porting Rockbox to an undocumented $9 AliExpress 'YP3' MP3 player with LLMs
items.author: jaydenmilne
items.content:
Rockbox is a wonderful old custom firmware project for a variety of MP3 players and iPods. Flashing rockbox to my Sansa E200 was a seminal moment for me: computers were everywhere, and if they didn’t do cool things, it was because no one had bothered to program them to do so. Looking back, that played no small part in my choice of career.

It seems like in 2026 there aren’t any cheap MP3 players that Rockbox supports though. Reverse engineering an embedded platform like this is one of the hardest things I can think of, and I had decided to pay the big bucks for one of those delicious subsidized token plans to try and push it as hard as I could, and I did have a dirt cheap $9 Aliexpress MP3 player lying around.

TL;DR: it ported Rockbox to a 512 KiB player, I was barely involved. Then, I had it build a re-usable toolkit/set of skills for future ports based on what worked from the first attempt approach, and Claude was able to get Rockbox running on another MP3 player (TS47) in 4 hours.

This is an unbranded player, sold under a variety of fake consonant soup brands on Amazon as well as Aliexpress. You can order them wholesale from Alibaba for less than $7 or so each.

NOTE: Before you run off and buy one, I have another rockbox port that is probably a week or two out, it is booting and stable, just needs more acceptance testing. This device is extremely similar but has 4 MiB PSRAM, so it has fewer compromises

I also have a stack of other random MP3 players I intend to repeat this with

If anyone gets credit for this rockbox port, it’s ilyakurdyukov - they figured out how to get it into ROM Download mode (Down + USB), and wrote a utility to dump / write flash. Then I could be a little slop kiddie and not have to use a soldering iron.

  • It costs $9. If it breaks buy another one.
  • There is a physical reset button, device is easily recoverable
  • Unbrickable (if you keep stock bootloader): holding down and resetting brings you into a DFU USB download mode.
  • Someone already figured out how to flash and interact with ROM DFU
  • That ROM DFU mode lets you poke flash and RAM.
  • Complete mystery meat Chinese “Smartlink SL6801” / Jointbees. Does not exist online
    • 2x Cortext-M4 r0p1 cpuID
    • 192 MHz (stock does not vary CPU freq). Has an FPU
    • Capable of Execute In Place (XIP) from flash, but no cache at all. Slow as dirt.
    • When XIP-ing code, cpu1 always waits behind cpu0 and can stall indefinitely if cpu0 is continuously fetching instructions from flash. Very easy to deadlock
  • 512 KiB plus about ~30 KiB for packets for the bluetooth radio.
  • 128x160 full color LCD (RGB565)
  • Only 5 buttons - a dpad with a center press (center press is power & wired to PMU)
  • Bluetooth (with an undocumented stack)

It has 512KiB of SRAM, and the smallest existing Rockbox target was 2 MiB, I was already scrolling Aliexpress for another one, but the LLM said “trust me bro I can make it happen” and I decided to try its luck.

  • While the hardware is cheap but functional, stock OS is painful to use
  • It regularly crashes and watchdogs when in USB transfer mode

After about a week it was booting a build of Rockbox on a crash diet - every single buffer had been cut to the bone, but it could start and play audio. Tuning, bug fixing, etc took another month or so.

I am not aware of anything that isn’t working hardware wise.

The main feature you lose is concurrency while playing music and plugins. Codecs and plugins are already loaded and swapped around at runtime with normal Rockbox, but on this player there is one shared 128 KiB arena for both, so starting a plugin stops music playback.

  • Only English is supported
  • No pitch/speed control, surround, crossfade
  • No dircache, so folders are read straight from SD card
    • Large folders are truncated by default at 256 (configurable from 32 to 512)
  • Playlists are capped at 400
  • Codecs: WMA Pro, Musepack (MPC), RealAudio (Cook), and the chiptune formats SID, NSF, VGM, KSS, HES, SGC, ASAP. WavPack (16-bit), (24-bit/96 kHz)
  • MP3 (up to 320 kbps), AAC/M4A (AAC+ too, HE-AAC v2 plays in mono), WMA, Opus (up to ~192 kbps), Ogg Vorbis, FLAC (stereo, up to 24-bit/96 kHz), ALAC, WAV, AIFF, AU, TTA, APE, Speex, MOD, SPC, AY, GBS, A52/AC3, ATRAC3, Shorten, ADX, VOX, SMAF.

  • The database has a new variant that is disk only and has synchronous, blocking updates (ie the player shows a loading screen and stops music when it refreshes and doesn’t refresh in background). I think it also cut the “songs by letter” menu.

    The database requests memory for its menus at runtime, and depending on the size of your theme it can refuse to open the menus.

  • Themes, without backgrounds. load and work, although heavy themes can cause the database to stop opening (handled gracefully with a warning)

  • Overnight Claude reverse engineered the bluetooth stack and wrote a bluetooth HAL for Rockbox. I asked it before I went to bed and it was working in the morning.

    No binary blobs are shipped: the bt stack is burned into chip ROM (not flash), and the YP3 bluetooth driver calls into the stack.

Most of the codecs run from SRAM as normal. MP3, AAC, WMA, Vorbis and Opus, however, wouldn’t fit in our arena nicely, so they run from flash.

But, our XIP flash is dirt slow, so lots of very careful profiling was done to move hot code loops back into SRAM. This kind of profiling had to be done all over Rockbox to get hot loops into SRAM - font rendering, alpha blending, scrolling, etc. This is where most of the “weeks of polishing” went.

Largely comparable to stock. I hooked the player up to the PC’s line in or fake bluetooth sink and set it to repeat Daft Punks . A script on the PC detected when it cut out.

21.29 hours wired, 20.07 on Bluetooth

20.07 hours wired, 19.3 on Bluetooth

There was some variation in the battery voltage at start, and this was just one run, so expect some variation.

Battery life is surprisingly impressive on this player,

I’m one of those software guys, I can’t solder or find UART pads to save my life. This was an entirely software only port; I haven’t ever opened mine up.

I hooked up ghidra-mcp and let it start pulling the firmware apart. It figured out how to inject tasks into the running RTOS (FreeRTOS) in bootloader mode. This allowed it to probe the hardware and even write drivers before attempting a Rockbox boot.

To be clear: this is . I have only glanced at some of the code it wrote. I contributed my approach to development and testing, was the PM and QA person, and the agent’s little meat robot to reboot it when it crashed or wander around my house with headphones on while it tuned the bluetooth radio. I haven’t doneC and firmware development for years.

Initially I let the same agent do the reverse engineering as implementation. Later I had it go through and rip out anything that wasn’t a hardware fact (ie a register) and re-did the drivers with a cleanroom setup. One dirty agent with Ghidra, one referee agent in between to make sure nothing leaks, and the implementation agent. Subsequent ports used a variation of this setup from the beginning

The most work I have done personally on this project is writing this blog post.

  • Webcam pointed at the screen, so the model could see what the player was doing and to work on the LCD drivers.

  • Webcam mic for bringing up the speaker

    (had to yell at Claude when it decided to start playing tones at 2 AM)

  • Headphone jack plugged into Line In on my PC (finally, I used it!!)

    This allowed it to test and tune audio output.

  • Bluetooth adapter. I plugged in a bluetooth adapter and gave it full reign for testing. It used Google’s Bumble python bluetooth stack to have the PC pretend to be headphones
  • Claude kept picking “We Will Rock You” as a test track. I choose to believe this is evidence of a subtle sense of humor when working on a Rockbox port

This port was started with Codex/Sol 5.6. It was making progress, but was incredibly risk averse and slow. It took it 5 days or so and dozens of manual resets on my part until it felt ready to flash something and boot it.

I should have told it how to figure out how to arm the watchdog and reboot into download mode itself sooner. Codex got it to showing the rockbox logo with buggy drivers stubbed out, but had clearly lost its mind in the meantime. I hadn’t been paying attention too closely, but as it had spun around it had:

  • Created 55 GB of files in 2,567 dirs. 3.87 million files total
  • 443 one off tool scripts, 384 documents written
  • an incredibly paranoid flasher that would check each block as it was written and took 15 minutes to write 2 MiB

    • This flashing script - and many other tool scripts - would check the sha256 of the documentation files they depended on to ensure nothing had changed.

      It’s kind of beautiful in its own insane way: this seems to be an attempt to work around multiple agents and memory limits. Madness though

  • An MCP server with tons of ceremony and tools around flashing things, running tests, etc

Claude immediately threw that garbage away and wrote like a few python scripts to use instead. Auto mode in claude code helped too.

The subsequent TS17 port went from me plugging it in to a usable alpha build in about 4 hours with Opus 5.5 (there was little to re-use from the YP3 other than scripts and skills).

Bidirectional Rockbox Dev Shell

This is one of the most valuable things it did. Rockbox has an existing one-way USB serial driver for logs. I had that extended to have dozens of little commands to drive the player, everything from injecting keypresses to taking screenshots to debugging the bluetooth radio.

This was critical for completely hands off development - I had it build a torture test suite in Python that would monkey-test the player for hours, pressing buttons at random. Many bugs were found doing this - including some in Rockbox upstream. At this point the player has hundreds of hours of bench testing under Rockbox - I could just leave it running and Claude would patiently watch the test logs for new failures to diagnose and fix.

An agent can reboot to recovery, flash firmware, reboot into Rockbox, run tests, see what is on the screen, hear what it is doing, completely on its own. Most of the development of this project happened while I was asleep.

For audio (and battery endurance testing) Claude had me set up a 3.5 mm splitter with one end going into the PC’s Line In and the other going into real headphones to provide an actual load.

Then I had it build a test suite and file that plays a variety of sweeps and test tones. I used an Apple lightning adapter to use as the ground truth for this setup, then used it to compare audio levels and frequency response.

My PC’s sound card is not high sensitivity equipment, but this is enough of a sanity check for me.

items.title: Freeing the iPod Nano 5G
items.author: rpm_conservatio
items.content:
A few years ago, CUB3D demonstrated unsigned code execution on the iPod nano 6G and 7G through , a font-based exploit. Whether the same approach would work on the 5G was still an open question.

I wanted to get Rockbox running on the nano 5G, so I set out to adapt the exploit. My motivation was simple: an up-to-date music player without an internet connection. I built a fully untethered boot chain that loads Rockbox from the nano 5G’s NAND, with no computer or button sequence needed after installation. I also found a way to make the existing exploit fully untethered on the nano 7G, and likely the 6G too.

Existing DFU exploits, including q3k’s wInd3x, provide code execution on the nano 5G, but booting custom code this way requires a computer each time. I used wInd3x to explore the device and develop a convenient, fully untethered exploit. The firmware details below refer to the latest nano 5G firmware, .

The nano 5G’s NAND flash appears through a flash translation layer (FTL) as a logical disk with 4 KiB sectors. Its partition table separates a small private area for persistent device state, a firmware partition containing boot programs and resources, and a data volume for user files. The firmware partition has a directory of named images; the fonts live inside , a resource volume formatted as FAT16.

The original chain combines a resource-validation bypass with a font-parser vulnerability. Apple’s firmware directory identifies the normal operating system as , the disk-mode program as , and the resource image containing fonts as . The disk-mode boot path does not request the resource signature check used by normal OS boot.

Swapping the and directory entries exploits that difference: selecting disk mode now launches Apple’s regular OS under the disk-mode policy. The OS still reads its fonts, but the bootloader has not required a valid signature for the modified resource image.

The font then triggers CVE-2010-1797, the FreeType CFF stack-overflow vulnerability also known through the exploit. A malformed font program corrupts the parser’s stack and redirects execution. My 5G port adapts that technique to the device’s font and execution context.

The swapped images remain on disk, but each restart still requires choosing disk mode with the device’s buttons. A normal boot selects the other entry. I wanted a better experience, with the modified font loading through the normal OS path.

Finding a bypass in the normal boot path

The bootloader is organized into EFI-style modules stored as Portable Executable (PE) images. The module that passes execution to the next boot stage decides whether to validate . It first asks the module for , which comes from an authenticated record in the private NAND partition.

The decisive branch is below. This is reconstructed C from the reverse-engineered routine, with unrelated fuse handling and protocol setup omitted.

A value of returns success before the resource-validation query. Bit 0 must remain clear: it is checked first, so would reject the boot attempt. Tracing the restore OS shows that it sets the status to during firmware transfer and clears it to at the end. This suggests an update-in-progress guard that prevents booting an incomplete installation.

Apple’s resource-mount path writes status only on the first successful boot, after has passed signature verification. My hypothesis is that this avoids repeating signature verification to shorten boot time or reduce energy use.

This is the second bypass. Instead of disguising the normal OS as disk mode, I can leave the firmware directory alone and supply a valid private record with bit 1 set. The normal boot path then accepts the modified resource image, and its font delivers code execution automatically.

The record lives in the private partition, identified by MBR type . On the 5G layout I examined, the partition begins at logical block 1, with 4 KiB blocks. The bootloader reads a 512-byte header from its start. The status-bearing format begins with the little-endian magic and has this layout:

The fields needed to understand the bypass
Three 32-bit words:
32-bit ; use
16-byte device-bound integrity tag

The integrity tag is device-specific, so creating and saving a valid PRVD record requires code execution on that iPod.

The tag is the first 16 bytes of the SHA-1 digest, encrypted with the device’s hardware AES UID key, selected through key slot 2. It authenticates the private header, but as the authentication is constructed on device we can falsify it if we have code execution.

Using emCORE to make it persistent

To inspect and update the private partition, I adapted , an older framework from freemyipod’s earlier iPod exploitation and boot work. It provided an existing USB-controlled environment to extend for the 5G.

I wrote the nano 5G NAND driver and integrated it into emCORE alongside the flash translation layer (FTL) and hardware AES access. I’ll cover the flash memory sequencer subsystem (FMSS), which enables NAND writes, in a future post. The FTL presents logical sectors over physical flash; it is the layer through which I read and write the private record and install the modified font.

The private-status tool verifies the existing header and tag, constructs the updated record, and obtains its new tag from the device. It rechecks the partition table and header before writing, then flushes the write and reads it back. The tool writes a complete 4 KiB logical sector even though the bootloader only consumes the smaller header. This works on nano 5G hardware.

Once the private record and modified font are installed, they remain in NAND across restarts. emCORE and the host computer are needed for the installation workflow, not for each subsequent boot.

A bootloader in less than 28 KB

Reaching the font parser automatically solved persistence. The next constraint was fitting something useful inside the font. I wanted it to load Rockbox from storage, so the payload needed a NAND driver, a flash translation layer, a filesystem reader, and enough startup code to hand off reliably.

From the font slot to the main payload ceiling
Subtract 78,312 font bytes
Fixed overhead, excluding the stubSubtract 1,056 font bytes, leaving 86,048
Each code byte uses three font bytes: ⌊86,048 ÷ 3⌋ = 28,682 code bytes
Subtract 808 code bytes for cleanup and handoff to the bootloader
28,682 − 808 =

To fit, I compiled with size and link-time optimizations and had the linker remove unused sections. The Rockbox kernel is stored on the device’s FAT32 partition and can be easily updated.

Taking control from the font parser

Code execution initially arrives in a damaged FreeType call frame. The stack has been corrupted, and Apple’s OS has left interrupts, DMA controllers, timers, caches, and address translation configured for its own use. Jumping straight into a large C program would carry that state into storage initialization.

I split the bootstrap into two images. The first is the 808-byte assembly stub at . Its job is to leave the parser context: mask IRQs and FIQs, switch to a private stack, stop inherited timer activity, quiesce DMA and clock domains, and clean up caches and the MMU before entering the main payload. It replaces the damaged stack and then jumps to the Rockbox kernel loader.

The second image is the main loader at . Its entry code disables the watchdog before starting the NAND scan, installs its own stack, and clears the uninitialized-data area before calling C. The watchdog matters because reconstructing the logical flash mapping can take several seconds; a reset in the middle would stop the boot before it ever found Rockbox.

This separation keeps the most fragile stage small. The assembly stub establishes a controlled execution environment; the main payload can then do the more substantial storage work in freestanding C.

Reading NAND and starting Rockbox

At the hardware level, the NAND driver uses FMSS, a programmable microcontroller, to communicate with the NAND chips. lemonjesus’s earlier work on the S5L8702 sequencer, published as , documents its instruction set and provides tools for inspecting and building bytecode. That research is important prior work for understanding this part of the storage hardware; my work here uses the sequencer to read NAND as part of the nano 5G boot path.

The loader first checks that the microsecond timer used for driver timeouts is running. It then initializes the read-only NAND and FTL stack, mounts the FAT filesystem, and opens . The core sequence follows the Rockbox bootloader’s own file-loading path:

The file loader checks the Rockbox model identifier and checksum, then leaves the executable image at . The final handoff keeps interrupts masked, cleans and invalidates caches, drains pending writes, and branches to that address. Rockbox’s startup code takes over from there. If storage, mounting, or image loading fails, the payload shows the failing stage on the LCD and stops.

On my nano 5G, the result is a cold, battery-powered boot straight into Rockbox, with no USB connection and no disk-mode button sequence. The PRVD partition setting skips validation and, when combined with the exploit, enables untethered boot straight into Rockbox. The main constraint is that the font payload is limited to 27,874 bytes. Installation and restoration procedures, along with the reverse-engineering notes and build details, are in the nano5g_bootstub and nano5g_emCORE repositories below.

I have confirmed that the private-data partition works the same way on the nano 7G, which suggests the method will likely work on the 6G too. I plan to get the nano 4G and 5G Rockbox ports into good shape before applying this method to the 6G and 7G.

items.title: GPT-6.2 Astra is the first model to beat Googlers' code golf records
items.author: bjin
items.content:
Back in 2015, when I was still at Google, there was a small group of code-golf enthusiasts spending hours trying to save just one byte on their solutions for weekly code-golf problems. No matter how hard you tried, there always seemed to be another Googler who found a shorter solution. And once a problem entered the challenge phase and every solution became public, it was always astonishing to read how brilliant other people's solutions were.

11 years later, LLMs are evolving fast. A recent OpenAI post ("Perplexity and Intelligence", https://openai.com/index/perplexity-and-intelligence/) described researchers watching a model solve open math problems one after another in a Slack thread. I started to wonder: how would frontier models compete with the records that a small group of brilliant minds created with hours of effort each week?

So I built this benchmark. Frontier models do find a lot of new approaches (and very brilliant ones) to solve these problems. For example, in two problems ("Surviving Queens" and "The Rolling Dice"), frontier models use complex numbers to solve them in Python and Ruby (both languages have built-in complex number support). And for the "(-5)-Smooth Numbers" problem, where you have to write code to list the first n positive integers of the form (-2)^x⋅(-3)^y⋅(-5)^z, most solutions build them with nested loops or by growing a set, then sort. GPT-6.2 Astra gets them all from powers of 4, and earns a sole best with this brilliant solution:

    g=lambda n:sorted(4**i%(2**999-5)%(2**49-3)for i in range(7000))[:n]
There is a dedicated section for this: https://bjin.github.io/go-codegolf-benchmark/#why/finding-a-...

It's nice to see GPT-6.2 Astra become the first frontier model to beat the human records in code golfing. Along with other frontier models, it finds a lot of interesting solutions that Googlers back in 2015 didn't. On the other hand, I also believe code golfing can be a good benchmark (not a comprehensive one, of course) for frontier models.

Code golfing rewards thinking differently, because a shorter solution usually comes from looking at the problem from a different angle. It also rewards running experiments, not just thinking: writing a search program to find a shorter expression, or exploring lesser-known features and functions in the target compiler, interpreter, or library. Human code golfers do this a lot, and no public training data tells a frontier model how to do so.

items.title: I joined the NTP Pool, but not with my Stratum 1 Pi
items.author: fortran77
items.content:
Before I get deep into the time-nuts rabbit hole, I figured I should share a little bit of the good time I now have in my studio, with everyone .

I posted a video about the setup today on YouTube:

I'd encourage anyone else interested in network time to contribute to the NTP Pool. However, there are some things you should know before contributing your own time services:

You don't need to go all out with a timing-grade GNSS module like I'm using. Heck, you don't even need GNSS-backed time at all!

The main requirements for hosting a node in the global NTP pool are:

  1. Keeping the system online (servers are only made active in the pool if they're online and serving good time consistently for a long period)
  2. Maintaining a good time—which can mean Stratum 1 GNSS service, but could also mean pulling time from a few other reliable time servers, and running as Stratum 2 or 3
  3. A stable IP address (IPv4 and/or IPv6), and a long-term commitment

Just 'testing the waters' in the Pool wastes resources—when you bring a new server online, it will take at least a few hours just to spin up all the tests to verify the server's providing a good time.

If you just want to operate your own time server, that's fine; the NTP Pool is a shared global resource, so joining it is a more of a commitment.

Two other important caveats:

  1. Your NTP server's IP address will be public
  2. NTP traffic will slowly decay, and some misconfigured systems could take months or even before they'll stop sending NTP traffic at your IP

The first caveat matters a lot to me: back when I exposed my home IP address trying to self-host this website on a cluster of Raspberry Pis, some doofus decided to DDoS my website—and was persistently doing so for the better part of a month.

I had to cycle my home IP, then put my site behind Cloudflare, just to protect my poor Pis (and eventually the VPS I now host it on).

Secure and Measurable Time

For those reasons, I chose to have two layers to my public time services:

  • : I have my Time Pi running in the studio, running a WireGuard tunnel to:
  • : A VPS I host with a cloud provider in St. Louis, to keep the latency down (ideally with fewer hops across the Internet, which leads to better time sync via NTP)

I include the Stratum 2 time server in my Stratum 1 time server's config as a source, so I can easily compare the Internet delay between the two servers, outside the WireGuard tunnel:

This provides me with the following graph:

I've been tracking my time in comparison to an NTP time server hosted at WWV in Ft. Collins, CO (pictured below), one of NIST's NTP servers in Boulder, CO, and Cloudflare.

For typical NTP configurations, you shouldn't single out time servers like this; I'm only doing it for long-term measurement (and I only poll the servers every 1024 seconds). Most systems should use pool addresses, as documented here.

The line for Cloudflare steps up and down sometimes, most likely due to BGP routing: as routes and servers change, packets between St. Louis and can take very different paths there and back.

Note: You might be looking for info on NTS, or Network Time Security—I haven't explored it much, so expect more on that at a later time. Currently the NTP Pool doesn't support NTS, though some have experimented with it. I'm okay with basic NTP and would recommend anyone with critical timing needs to use other time sources as well (don't rely on NTP!).

Chrony and GPS time tweaks

My Time Pi is not only serving as a Stratum 1 timing reference for my public NTP server, it's also my primary reference for local time in the studio.

The TimeHAT on top does most of the heavy lifting, with its built-in Intel i226 NIC. The i226 includes hardware timestamping, essential for accurate PTP timing on the LAN. To deliver the most accurate time possible, I installed a timing-grade GNSS receiver (u-blox ZED-F9T, built to the M.2 NGFF Sync Module specification.

The entire configuration (for both servers) is managed by Ansible in my time-pi project.

Using the i226, I'm able to discipline the NIC's hardware clock (called the 'PHC', or 'PTP Hardware Clock') , directly from the GPS module's PPS (Pulse Per Second) pin. Using linuxptp's tool, I can discipline the PHC to within tens-of-ns of UTC, and distribute that time to other PTP-aware computers on the LAN.

The time on the PHC is shared to my Pi's system clock using inside Chrony, instead of , because I was experiencing a weird 200ms jump every so often. Chrony then disciplines the system clock, but this can only be accurate to about a microsecond, because the pulse goes through the PCIe bus, which adds latency I can't measure.

I'm actually trying to make this latency more measurable, since GPIO is routed through the RP1 chip deterministically. See ahmadexp's rp1-ptp-pps utility PR. PTM could reduce the error between the NIC's PHC and the system clock to a few ns, but the BCM2712 SoC on the Pi doesn't support it.

One other quirk I ran into was Debian's default sourcedir /run/chrony-dhcp directive, which was picking up another NTP server via DHCP, causing to stampede my accurate GNSS-derived time from with a far-less-accurate time from a public NTP server! (This was another motivation behind moving clock steering to instead of .)

I'm hosting my public Stratum 2 server with Oxtrys, a VPS provider I'd never used before—and one thing I was nervous about was how they'd react to a VPS handling only UDP packets like this.

Some automated firewalls shut down public NTP servers because NTP traffic may like abuse. I wondered if that was the case late on the night of November 16, because the server dropped offline while I was writing this blog post:

But looking at the logs further, it seems an unattended upgrade installed a new Debian kernel, then rebooted the server, and the new kernel caused problems. For now the server still runs automatic upgrades, but leaves reboots to me.

Oxtrys' live chat support has been responsive enough, though their account dashboard is broken until November 22, so it doesn't list my server's out-of-band management options.

As you can see in the graph above, the NTP Pool monitors have slowly brought the server's score back up past '10', at which point it can serve time in the pool again. It takes maybe 6–12 hours to recover if the server's been down long enough.

I've certainly learned a lot at every stage of this journey: NTP is loaded with utility, and is currently an essential piece of global timing infrastructure. I think I know about 1% (probably less) of what there is to know about hosting a public NTP server, and hopefully I can share more as I increase that to a few more percentage points!

I'm thankful to all the other NTP Pool operators, as well as all the timelords who built and manage massive NTP endpoints like , , etc.
